articles.title: ‘Green Room’ Director Remembers Patrick Stewart as a ‘F—ing Sweetheart’ and Credits Him for Rescuing the Film: He ‘Swooped Down’ ‘Into Our Cruddy Ass Movie and Saved Us’
articles.summary: “Green Room” writer and director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to late actor Patrick Stewart, who starred in the film and whom he credits with saving the day when they were “close to shutting down,” during a 10th-anniversary screening of the 2015 film in Los Angeles on Friday.
body: Then, “Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” said Saulnier. “And in a whirlwind about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage, ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’

He continued: “Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit; we moved forward. And I thank him for just taking that leap and making ‘Green Room’ a thing.”

Saulnier remembered the actor as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, a kind leader to our whole cast,” and recounted his idea to add “a little something” to one scene: “I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, “Fuck!” And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ Permission granted, sir,” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”

articles.title: Frank Miller on Why He’s Relieved There Are Fewer Comic Book Adaptations Now: They Were ‘Really in Danger of Losing Their Souls’
articles.summary: Comic book writer and screenwriter Frank Miller – whose work includes “300,” “Sin City” and “Batman: The Dark Knight Returns” – returned this week to Lucca Comics and Games, an event that spans the gamut of geek culture and pop entertainment.
body: Variety spoke to Miller about politics, art and why he’s relieved there are fewer comic book movies this year.

Would you agree that there has been a slight dip in the comic book to movie pipeline? I would hope so. Yeah, really. It had really gotten so out of control that comics had started losing much of their own identity. I have been arguing vehemently for comics to start asserting their own purpose again and asserting their own identity as a literary form.

Do you think there were too many comic book artists and writers aiming for movie and TV deals? Oh, without question. Just because the appeal of not just the money, but the fame, respect and glory of working in the most powerful medium in history is undeniable, but I think that it was a little too heady a wine, in that comics were really in danger of losing their souls in the process.

articles.title: ‘Before the Rain’ Director Milcho Manchevski on Tokyo Competition Title ‘Sister Brother Manhole Cover,’ Whistleblowing and the ‘Death of Beauty’ in Cinema
articles.summary: Milcho Manchevski, the North Macedonian director whose 1994 debut “Before the Rain” won Venice’s Golden Lion and earned an Oscar nomination, is back in competition at the Tokyo International Film Festival with “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” a project stalled for years after he accused his…
body: “I wanted to tell a story about a kind of love that is rarely at the center of films, yet it is so beautiful: the love between a brother and a sister,” Manchevski tells Variety. “It can be fierce, complicated, sometimes painful, but also unconditional like no other type of love.”

The director also took inspiration from traditional Macedonian songs about sisterly love, which he calls poignant and at times shocking. Of Malina and Viktor, he says: “They are far from ideal people. But they are deserving of understanding and affection. I am interested in people as they are, with their contradictions, not as examples of how people should behave. Idealized characters make for bad movies.”

The siblings break the law and sometimes make terrible mistakes, but Manchevski says he had no wish to turn them into objects of pity. He sees the pair’s refusal to think of themselves as victims as a way of reclaiming their own story.

body: When it debuted in theaters last weekend, “Klara and the Sun” landed at a staggering No. 15 with just $720,000 from 880 locations, and Sony scaled back its theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as a “ calamitous ” and “strained, whimsical comedy that’s ruinous.”

Jenna Ortega, who stars as the film’s titular android, also recently revealed in a Vogue interview that she doesn’t read reviews of her films because “that would send me into a psychosis of some sort” or check the box office updates when her team sends them her way because “I don’t want it to become a numbers thing.”

articles.title: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry
articles.summary: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more. Man’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend…
body: “A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”

A 2024 study of US Google searches noted an increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.

articles.title: Michael Douglas Shares Update on Jack Nicholson: “He’s Well. He Has Disappeared”
articles.summary: "I still see him, but he is fine," the 'Basic Instinct' actor said of the three-time Oscar winner who has stayed out of the spotlight in recent years.
body: Michael Douglas is sharing a rare update on Jack Nicholson, who has largely remained out of the spotlight in recent years.
During an appearance to promote his memoir One Helluva Ride in Swansea, the Basic Instinct actor was asked about his relationship with Nicholson.
“I would have liked to have acted with Jack,” Douglas said, per The Independent. “He’s not working any more. He’s well. He has disappeared. I know that.”
Douglas is 82, and Nicholson is 89. The two actors only professionally collaborated on 1975’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, which Douglas produced and Nicholson starred in.

articles.title: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
articles.summary: The second series of the hit show reached its finale on Friday, attracting a whopping 11.2 million live viewers.
body: The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.
Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the £83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.
"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.
The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.

articles.title: The 5 Best Home Projectors for Movie Buffs, From 4K to Portable Picks
articles.summary: For movie lovers inspired by the IMAX spectacle of this year’s biggest blockbusters, these projectors offer a cinematic upgrade for your home.
body: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission.

Christopher Nolan may prefer you see his films in IMAX, but your living room has other plans. As Hollywood continues to champion the theatrical experience, advances in home entertainment technology are making it easier than ever to bring a little movie theater magic home, minus the overpriced popcorn and the person checking their phone three rows ahead.

Of course, not all projectors deserve top billing. A high-end 4K model might be ideal for watching visually ambitious blockbusters, while a portable 1080p option could be all you need for streaming your favorite series or hosting an outdoor movie night. Brightness, picture quality and the distance between your projector and screen are all worth considering before making the investment.

articles.title: Before Bonanza, Michael Landon Was In This Underrated '50s Western Series' Pilot
articles.summary: Michael Landon's small role in this pilot for a '50s Western TV series played a part in eventually landing him a career-making turn on Bonanza.
body: Long before he was Little Joe Cartwright on "Bonanza" or Charles Ingalls on "Little House on the Prairie," Michael Landon was Sandy Ray on "The Restless Gun." Not that anyone remembers this tiny role on a TV pilot that aired all the way back in 1957. But many might remember the series which it spawned, even though Landon himself didn't end up as part of the main cast.

In 1957, Landon was still trying to make a name for himself. By the time he was cast on "The Restless Gun," then, he had a fair few credits to his name but was yet to break through. He was also no stranger to the TV Western, having appeared in two episodes of "The Adventures of Jim Bowie" and an episode of the now-forgotten '50s gem that completely changed television, "Cheyenne."
